evidence.source: Academia Sinica, Ancient Chinese Character Database
evidence.text: The database labels the graph forms as oracle-bone, bronze, and small-seal script. Its explanation identifies the oracle-bone and bronze forms as a tall building: roof above, tower in the middle, and wall below; it says the small-seal form simplified the tower element to 口. This supports a building interpretation, but the database does not provide dated individual attestations in the accessible text.
evidence.title: 漢字「京」：字形演變

evidence.source: Taiwan Ministry of Education, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.text: The entry reproduces the Shuowen account: 京 is a very high man-made mound, analyzed there as a reduced 高 plus a vertical stroke indicating height. It records early textual examples for an artificial mound in the Book of Odes and in the History of the Three Kingdoms, and gives separate senses including ‘large’, granary, equal, capital, large-number unit, and a grave/mound reading. Its gloss list does not establish the chronology or semantic links among these senses. The entry explicitly distinguishes Shuowen’s explanation from its other dictionary senses.
evidence.title: [A00065] 京 - 教育部《異體字字典》

evidence.source: Chinese University of Hong Kong, Multi-function Chinese Character Database
evidence.text: The database reports a high platform / tall tower interpretation and quotes Shuowen’s high-mound analysis. It also gives a related-size interpretation (large) and reports 郭沫若’s comparisons linking 京 to large mounds, granaries, animals, and strength. These are dictionary interpretations, not a demonstrated dated chain from mound to capital.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫: 京

evidence.source: 公益財団法人 日本漢字能力検定協会, Kanjipedia
evidence.text: This dictionary calls 京 pictographic and interprets it as a house built on a high hill. It proposes that ancient people worshipped a deity on the hill and lived around it, explaining the ‘capital’ sense, with ‘large’ as a further extension. This is a competing semantic account; the page does not give dated evidence establishing that sequence.
evidence.title: 京 | 漢字一字 | 漢字ペディア

evidence.source: Taiwan Ministry of Education, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.text: The entry cites 詩經·小雅·甫田, “曾孫之庾，如坻如京,” with Mao’s Han-period gloss “京，高丘也” (‘京, a high mound’). It also cites 管子·輕重丁 for a granary sense, 左傳·莊公二十二年 for “equal/compare,” and 白居易·琵琶行 for capital-city use. The latter is a Tang poem; this is an attestation by cited work, not an exact manuscript date. The sources available here do not establish when capital use began or whether it arose through mound-to-settlement semantic extension, another path, or a distinct word sense.
evidence.title: [A00065] 京 - 教育部《異體字字典》

evidence.text: The chart includes U+4EAC 京. The requested character-specific Unihan endpoint could not be opened in the web tool; local Unihan_Readings.txt row U+4EAC reports kMandarin jīng. This is current reading metadata, not evidence for ancient sound or a proposed sound-component relation.

evidence.source: Unicode Consortium, Unicode Standard Version 17.0 CJK chart
evidence.text: The chart includes U+666F 景. Local Unihan_Readings.txt row U+666F reports kMandarin jǐng, while the local Baxter–Sagart data give 景 *C.qraŋʔ and 京 *[k]raŋ. 景 is a possible comparison raised in the dossier’s related etymological material, but no inspected source here establishes it as a phonetic component of 京; the differing readings are not by themselves proof of sound relation.
evidence.title: The Unicode Standard, Version 17.0: CJK Unified Ideographs

evidence.source: Baxter and Sagart, supplementary Old Chinese reconstruction data
evidence.field: 京 and 景: readings and notation
evidence.text: The authors describe their 2014 version 1.1 table as presenting Old Chinese reconstructions, Middle Chinese transcription, Mandarin pinyin, and glosses; they explain that square brackets mark uncertainty in segment identity. Local sources/baxter-sagart/baxtersagart.tsv exact rows 1728 and 1736 preserve 京 *[k]raŋ ‘hill; capital city’ and 景 *C.qraŋʔ ‘bright; image’. These notations must remain distinct; the local row for 景 has a different reconstruction and entering form. No evidence here makes 景 a component of 京.

gaps: No inspected source supplied dated individual oracle-bone examples or a dated earliest use for the capital-city sense. Academia Sinica labels the script stages and explains graph shape but does not expose dates for individual 京 attestations in the accessible text.

The evidence supports competing graphic/semantic readings: high built structure or platform, Shuowen’s high man-made mound, and a Japanese dictionary’s hilltop shrine/settlement explanation for ‘capital’. The semantic route to capital remains unproven by dated links.

The Ming/Qing received dictionary quotations cite older works, but do not provide manuscript witnesses or exact composition dates for all senses. Do not derive a chronology from their order in the gloss list.
No sound component is established for 京 in this research. 景 and 高 are comparisons in sources, not demonstrated components; phonological resemblance alone does not settle graphic composition.

The requested official Unicode character-specific Unihan pages for 京 and 景 were attempted but inaccessible through the web tool. The official Unicode chart and local sources/unihan/Unihan_Readings.txt rows 31627 and 89743 were checked; local rows are not treated as external evidence. The full local Unihan_Readings.txt was available, so the HSK extract was not needed.

The repository contains sources/baxter-sagart/baxtersagart.tsv, not the packet’s optional alternate path sources/baxter-sagart/baxtersagart.tsv? The exact local rows were checked: 京 row 1728, 景 rows 1736–1737. No external source for a competing Zhengzhang transcription was verified here.

Only one candidate image was verified as a depiction of 京 with reusable rights. Commons also lists other script-stage variants, but no individual direct image file for a later stage was opened and verified in this run.

The direct SVG fetches produced tool-level errors; URLs are recorded as direct links from the inspected Commons descriptions, not as successfully fetched image contents. No claim of pixel inspection is made.
The Commons oracle-style vector cites hanziyuan.net record B08320 as its source; its file page does not describe it as an artifact photograph. It is a modern vector redraw.
